label: Human
plain: The law inventory names its candidate proteins by their human genes, so the human side of the protein atlas is the inventory's own.

modelled.text: Cells models a generic cell and a sheet of such cells, with laws whose candidate proteins are named by their human genes; that generic cell is the one drawn. No human cell type, organ or body is modelled yet. The first human cell type is designed, not modelled: a ventricular heart cell, whose laws follow O'Hara and Rudy's model of 2011 (the endocardial cell). Its design note is on main, and its status there reads proposed, with its choices decided by D184 (decisions D183 and D184, 16 November 2026); nothing of it is built yet. The heart and the body are placeholder outlines.

record.where: D183: The human cardiac law set is brought forward; D184: The human cardiac law set's choices
Status: PROPOSED, 16 November 2026; its choices decided by D184

levels.note: The cell drawn is a generic animal cell, as one of a layer; it is not a model of a human cell type. Its shape and its sizes are the picture's choice: six flat sides where it meets its neighbours, about 20 µm across.

Its flat-sided shape is the picture's choice

levels.note: The sheet is the one Cells simulates: a single layer of coupled cells. It stands for no particular human tissue.

notes.text: The sheet Cells simulates: a single layer of coupled cells

levels.label: Heart
levels.note: The outline drawn is a human heart with its great vessels, as a placeholder. The heart is the picture's choice of organ: a paper on the injured heart is the user's high priority among the published models to reproduce (14 November 2026). No heart is modelled. The sheet of cells is drawn on the chest over the heart so that the scales follow one another; it is not heart tissue, and the heart's own cells are not modelled. The heart is drawn about 12 cm long, 9 cm broad and 6 cm thick, the size that an anatomy textbook of 1918 gives for an adult's heart; the sizes of the vessels are the picture's choice.

levels.label: Whole body
levels.note: The outline drawn is a human body lying on its back, 1.7 m long, as a placeholder. The sheet of cells is drawn on the chest for the scales only. Its length is the picture's choice, within the range of mean adult heights that one study gives, about 1.4 to 1.8 m; the body's proportions are the picture's choice too.

facts.label: Nucleus
facts.value: nuclei isolated from HeLa cells, a human cell line, in the paper's column “HeLa (fresh)”, were 17.18 ± 0.39 µm wide (the mean of their long and short axes, by light microscopy) and 16.20 ± 0.48 µm high (by atomic force microscopy), mean ± s.e.m. of 21 nuclei; the same table's column “HeLa” gives 12.73 ± 0.54 µm wide and 10.91 ± 0.59 µm high (23 nuclei). These are nuclei taken out of the cell, not nuclei measured in an intact cell

facts.label: Mitochondrion
facts.value: the paper's normal mitochondria, beside the giant ones it studies, in the liver of people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, measured in three dimensions, were 0.55 ± 0.15 µm wide and 1.18 ± 0.59 µm long, total means ± S.D. combining the measurements from each patient (four cells from each patient, 16 cells in all); its giant mitochondria were 0.64 ± 0.24 µm wide and 3.99 ± 1.68 µm long

facts.label: Lysosome
facts.value: single lysosomes of HeLa cells, each measured on its own by electron microscopy guided by fluorescence: one “a spherical shape with an approximate diameter of 560 nm” (0.56 µm), others 0.56 × 0.56 × 0.51 µm, 0.55 × 0.58 × 0.62 µm and 0.66 × 0.69 × 0.50 µm. These are single examples, not a measure of many

facts.label: COPI vesicle
facts.value: dots containing COPI (coatomer) in HeLa cells, seen by STED fluorescence microscopy and sized by fitting each image (a 2D Lorentzian), were 126 ± 15 nm (0.126 µm), n = 181: an apparent size from a light microscope's fit, not an electron microscope's; COPI vesicles made in vitro measured 114 ± 11 nm (n = 64) the same way

facts.label: Peroxisome
facts.value: an encyclopedia's general range, not a measurement in one cell type: “Peroxisomes are small (0.1–1 μm diameter) organelles”

gray1918.text: Gray H, Lewis WH (1918) Anatomy of the Human Body, 20th edition. Lea and Febiger, Philadelphia. It gives the adult heart as about 12 cm long, 8 to 9 cm broad at its broadest part and 6 cm thick. Read in the text of the Internet Archive's scan of the book.
gray1918.licence: Public domain: published in the United States in 1918. The Internet Archive's record of the scan gives its copyright status as not in copyright.

ncdrisc2016.text: NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (2016) A century of trends in adult human height. eLife 5:e13410. Mean adult heights by country and year of birth: the shortest were women born in Guatemala in 1896, 140.3 cm, and the tallest Dutch men born late in the twentieth century, above 182.5 cm.

lherbette2017.text: Lherbette M and others (2017) Atomic Force Microscopy micro-rheology reveals large structural inhomogeneities in single cell-nuclei. Scientific Reports 7:8116. Table 1, the columns “HeLa (fresh)” and “HeLa” (mean ± s.e.m.; the width by light microscopy as the mean of the long and short axes, the height by atomic force microscopy), and the Methods on how the width was measured. Read on the journal's page.

shami2021.text: Shami GJ and others (2021) Three-dimensional ultrastructure of giant mitochondria in human non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Scientific Reports 11:3319. Results, the sentence that begins “On average GM were 3.5 × longer”, which gives the widths and lengths of the giant (GM) and normal (NM) mitochondria; the Methods give the data as total means ± S.D. combining the measurements from each patient, four cells from each (16 cells in total). Read on the journal's page.
